audit.recode_to: If the record is kept as a K'iche' variant at all: 01 001 0001 00001 (fixed final primary, single stress; light non-root final syllables extrametrical per Henderson 2012:26) — i.e. identical to kich1262's coding of record, which is why merging is the cleaner action.
audit.deciding_source_year: Wikipedia (read 2026-08-31; sentence uncited); displayed source Henderson 2012
audit.reasoning: (1) Identity: Glottolog marks kich1263 as a retired/bookkeeping entry (ISO qxi 'San Andrés Quiché', merged into quc 2009-01-16; only ref is the ISO change request); the catalog already counts it under kich1262 (RETIRED_ALIAS, ruling IDENTITY-MAPPED-DIALECT-VARIANT). The V42 'dialect-variant fence' on kich1262 says the five retired-code records 'report final primary + alternating secondaries' as if from dialect surveys, but their deciding text is one uncited Wikipedia sentence about K'iche' generally, copied to all five codes — there is no dialect-specific evidence, so the record is a duplicate of kich1262 carrying a conflicting rule. (2) Rule: every primary source opened gives plain word-final primary stress and no rhythmic secondaries — Larsen 1988:21 (held) 'Stress in Quiché always falls on the final syllable'; Henderson 2012:26-27 (fetched sources, quote verbatim) final in the prosodic word a

sources.quote: "K'ICHEE' STRESS GENERALIZATION: Stress falls on the final syllable of a prosodic word, unless that syllable is light non-root material, in which case it falls on the final root syllable." (Henderson 2012, preprint p. 26, ex. (82); "The first part of the generalization is that stress is attracted to the right edge of the prosodic word." (same page). sources.citation: Wood, Elizabeth Anne. 2025. Predictable vowel deletion in content words and variable vowel deletion in function words in Chichicastenango K'iche'. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 55(3): 465-502. doi:10.1017/S0025100325100765 (open access)
sources.quote: 'Primary stress is word-final in non-verbs in Chichicastenango K'iche', with the exclusion of two extrametrical suffixes: the superlative /-@l@X/ and the suffix /-Ik/ ... Stress is non-final in some unadapted Spanish loanwords' (p. 467). 'In verbs, stress is sensitive to vowel quality and syllable shape. Stress falls on the left-most syllable containing either a tense vowel or a coda, or if there are none, on the final syllable. The stress domain excludes most inflectional morphemes' (p. 468). No secondary stress. Refines the plain-final picture for one (innovative) dialect; says nothing about

sources.citation: Nielsen, Kuniko. 2005. Kiche intonation. UCLA Working Papers in Phonetics 104: 45-60. escholarship.org/uc/item/52n7344j
sources.quote: 'Stress in Kiche is always word-final (Larsen, 1988). Stressed syllables are marked by pitch, duration, intensity, and loudness. Most importantly, Kiche stress is marked by a rise of the fundamental frequency (F0) on the stressed syllable.' Clitics do not shift stress; some recent loans (mángo, pláto) non-final. Only phrase-level: an AP-initial H* 'rhythmic high' when an AP exceeds 3-4 syllables (p. 47) — not word-level alternating stress.
